title: Number Strings
subtitle: A purposefully sequenced set of related problems, posed one at a time, where each problem helps with the next — nudging students toward a target strategy.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Fosnot & Dolk, Young Mathematicians at Work (minilessons / strings) · Pamela Harris, Building Powerful Numeracy · NCTM, Principles to Actions.

blocks.text: A **string** is a short, carefully ordered sequence of problems — posed and discussed one at a time — designed so that the earlier “helper” problems give students a foothold for the harder “target” problem.

The sequence is the teaching. Students aren’t told a strategy; the *design* of the string leads them to notice a relationship and use it. Solve `1/2 + 1/2`, then `1/2 + 1/4`, then `3/4 + 1/4` — and the move “make a whole” emerges naturally before they hit `3/4 + 5/6`.

They’re cousins. A **Number Talk** usually centers on *one* problem and many strategies. A **Number String** is a *designed sequence* of several problems where the order does the work — the helper problems are chosen to make a target strategy almost inevitable. Reach for a string when you have a specific strategy or big idea in mind.

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Build fluency from understanding
Use & connect representations
Facilitate meaningful discourse
**Pose the first (helper) problem.** Students solve mentally; share and record strategies.
**Pose the next,** chosen to connect to the one before. “Does the last problem help here?”
**Keep going up the string,** recording so the pattern becomes visible on the board.
**Reach the target problem.** Students apply the strategy the string built.
**Name the strategy & the connections.** “What did you notice across these?”

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “The last one helps because…”
Strategies recorded so the pattern shows
Students noticing the relationship themselves
The target problem solved with the new strategy

no.title: We should *not* see
items: Problems treated as unrelated / random
The teacher announcing the strategy up front
Racing through without recording connections
A string so long it loses focus (keep it 4–6)
**The helper problems are the access** — every student can enter the first, easy problem, and the scaffolding is built into the sequence.
**Strategies are honored, not imposed** — students arrive at the target idea through their own noticing, which builds disposition.
**Public recording** of each step supports working memory and gives multilingual learners a visual anchor for the discussion.

blocks.text: Keep strings short (4–6 problems) and pose them *one at a time* — never show the whole list at once, or you lose the “does the last one help?” reasoning. Ready-made strings exist for most 6–8 topics.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Fosnot & Dolk, Young Mathematicians at Work · Pamela Harris, Building Powerful Numeracy · NCTM, Principles to Actions.

blocks.text: An **Opener routine** — reach for it when you have a **specific strategy or big idea** you want students to build, and a sequence can lead them to it.

Choose a Number String over a Number Talk when you want direction: the string is engineered to surface one target strategy (make-a-whole, halving/doubling, using a unit rate). It’s also a great way to revisit prior content with purpose, which is why it lives under “spiral & retrieve.”

blocks.title: How a string is built: helpers → target

blocks.text: Start from the **target problem** and the strategy you want. Then work backward to design 3–5 **helper problems** that each make the next one easier and, together, make the target strategy the natural move. The sequence is the lesson plan.
Designing a string in five minutes

items: **Name the target** problem and the strategy you want surfaced.
**Write 2–3 helpers** that build toward it — each a small step from the last.
**Open with an easy entry** everyone can do mentally.
**Plan your recording** (a number line, equations stacked) so the pattern is visible by the target.

headers: The string (pose one at a time)
rows: Use benchmarks & complements instead of jumping to a common denominator.
Build percents from 10% and 5%; transfer to a new whole.
`$6 for 4` → cost of 2 → cost of 1 → cost of 10
Unit rate as a reusable tool; scaling up and down.
Subtraction as distance/direction; subtracting a negative.
“Of” as scaling; connect fraction & decimal forms.

blocks.title: Run it one problem at a time

blocks.text: The reasoning (“does the last one help?”) only happens if students can’t see what’s coming. Reveal each problem in turn, discuss, record, *then* reveal the next. Never post the whole string at once.

items: **The opening problem is the access** — make it genuinely easy so every student is in from the first move.
**Record on a number line or visual** so the pattern is seen, not just stated.
**Let students name what they noticed** across the string — arriving at the strategy themselves is the disposition win.

blocks.text: The “helpers to target” design is the same thinking behind **Thin-Slicing** in Core Instruction — sequencing tasks in small steps so students extend their own thinking. Strings build the instinct in the opener; thin-slicing scales it to a full task.
